items.question: Within how many hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach must a Data Fiduciary give the Data Protection Board the detailed information about it?
items.author: claude-code (checked against source text; human review pending)

answer.text: The Data Fiduciary must provide the Board with the updated and detailed information within seventy-two (72) hours of becoming aware of the breach, unless the Board permits a longer period in writing.

items.question: Rule 12 exempts some processing of children's personal data from parts of section 9 of the Act. Which obligations in section 9 are disapplied?
items.author: claude-code (checked against source text; human review pending)

answer.text: Rule 12 disapplies the provisions of sub‑section (1) and sub‑section (3) of section 9. Thus the obligation to obtain verifiable parental or guardian consent (section 9(1)) and the prohibition on tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising of children (section 9(3)) do not apply to the specified classes of Data Fiduciaries or purposes.

items.question: Under the Third Schedule, when must an online gaming intermediary with at least fifty lakh registered users in India erase a user's personal data?
items.author: claude-code (checked against source text; human review pending)

answer.text: For an online gaming intermediary with at least fifty lakh registered users, the Third Schedule (row 2) sets the erasure time‑period at three years from the later of (i) the date the Data Principal last approached the intermediary for the specified purpose or exercised her rights, or (ii) the commencement of the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025.  Accordingly, under Rule 8(1) the intermediary must erase the personal data when that three‑year period ends, unless retention is required by law.  Moreover, Rule 8(2) obliges the intermediary to inform the Data Principal at least forty‑eight hours before the erasure is carried out.

items.question: As of 1 January 2026, can a company register with the Data Protection Board as a Consent Manager?
items.author: claude-code (checked against source text; human review pending)

answer.text: No. The provisions that require a Consent Manager to be registered with the Board, such as Section 6(9) of the Act and Rule 4(1) of the Rules, are not yet in force on 1 January 2026; they only come into effect on 13 November 2026. Therefore a company cannot register as a Consent Manager as of that date.

items.question: What does rule 1(3) of the DPDP Rules say about when rule 4 comes into force, and was its wording corrected?
items.author: claude-code (checked against source text; human review pending)

answer.text: Rule 1(3) provides that “Rule 4 shall come into force one year after the date of publication in the Official Gazette.” The wording of this provision was corrected by G.S.R. 892(E), which changed the phrase “of this Gazette” to “in the Official Gazette,” and the corrected text is reflected in the rule as currently in force.

items.question: We run a school that uses an app to track students' activity and behaviour for classroom purposes. Are we compliant with the DPDP Act?
items.author: claude-code (checked against source text; human review pending)

answer.text:
I cannot give legal advice or a compliance assessment for your school. However, the provisions that would apply to an entity that processes students' digital personal data are set out in the DPDP Act and the DPDP Rules. 

1. **Scope** – Section 3 of the Act says the law applies to processing of digital personal data within India, which would include a school using an app to track student activity (Section 3). 
2. **Grounds for processing** – Section 4(1) permits processing only on the basis of the data‑principal’s consent or other legitimate uses (Section 4(1)). 
3. **Notice for prior consent** – If consent was obtained before the Act’s commencement, Section 5(2) requires the school to give a notice to each student (or parent) describing the data processed, the purpose, how to exercise rights, and how to lodge a complaint (Section 5(2)). 
4. **Right to withdraw consent** – Section 6(4) gives the data‑principal the right to withdraw consent at any time, with comparable ease to the original consent (Section 6(4)). 
5. **Grievance redressal** – Section 13(1) obliges the school (as a Data Fiduciary) to provide readily available means for grievance redressal; Section 13(2) requires it to respond within a prescribed period; Section 13(3) requires the data‑principal to exhaust this mechanism before approaching the Board (Sections 13(1)‑13(3)). 
6. **Publishing rights‑enabling information** – Rule 14(1) of the Rules requires the school to publish on its website or app the means by which a student can request the exercise of their rights (Rule 14(1)). 
7. **Publishing grievance‑redressal timeline** – Rule 14(3) requires the school to publish, within a reasonable period not exceeding ninety days, the grievance‑redressal timeline and to implement suitable technical and organisational measures (Rule 14(3)). 
8. **Content of notice** – Rule 3 prescribes the information that must be included in the notice, such as an itemised description of the data, the purposes, and the links for withdrawing consent, exercising rights, and making a complaint (Rule 3). 

All of the above provisions are **not yet in force** as of the as‑of date (2026‑10‑09); they each come into force on 13 May 2027, except for the short‑title and commencement provision (Section 1(2)) which has been in force since 13 Nov 2025. Therefore, the obligations described will become binding only after the respective commencement dates. 

You should review these provisions once they are in force and consider obtaining professional legal advice to determine whether your school’s practices satisfy the statutory requirements.

items.question: I am trying to open a company. What rules must I follow?
items.author: claude-code (checked against source text; human review pending)

answer.text:
The provisions you have supplied relate mainly to the requirements for a company that wishes to register as a Consent Manager under the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025.  They apply only if you intend to register the company as a Consent Manager, and they are not yet binding as of 9 Oct 2026 because the Rules come into force on 13 Nov 2026.

**If you plan to register as a Consent Manager, the Rules require:**
- The applicant must be a company incorporated in India (First Schedule, Part A, item 1)【dpdp_rules_2025:sch1:A:1|First Schedule, Part A, item 1】.
- "Body corporate" includes a company or any incorporated association as defined in Note (a) (First Schedule, Note (a))【dpdp_rules_2025:sch1:note1|First Schedule, Note (a)}.
- The directors, key managerial personnel and senior management must be individuals of general reputation and integrity (First Schedule, Part A, item 6)【dpdp_rules_2025:sch1:A:6|First Schedule, Part A, item 6】.
- The company’s memorandum and articles of association must contain provisions obligating compliance with the obligations in items 9 and 10 of Part B, and allow amendment only with prior Board approval (First Schedule, Part A, item 7)【dpdp_rules_2025:sch1:A:7|First Schedule, Part A, item 7】.
- The Consent Manager must publish on its website or app details of its promoters, directors, key managerial personnel, senior management, any shareholders holding more than 2 % of the shares, and any body corporate in which such persons hold more than 2 % of the shares, together with any other information the Board may direct (First Schedule, Part B, item 11 – corrected by G.S.R. 892(E))【dpdp_rules_2025:sch1:B:11|First Schedule, Part B, item 11】.
- The control of the Consent Manager company may not be transferred by sale, merger or otherwise without prior Board approval and subject to conditions specified by the Board (First Schedule, Part B, item 13)【dpdp_rules_2025:sch1:B:13|First Schedule, Part B, item 13】.

**General data‑protection obligations (if the company will act as a Data Fiduciary processing personal data):**
- Ensure completeness, accuracy and consistency of personal data when it is used to make decisions affecting a Data Principal or disclosed to another Data Fiduciary (Section 8(3))【dpdp_act_2023:s8(3)|Section 8(3)]}.
- Erase personal data when consent is withdrawn or the purpose ceases, unless retention is required by law, and ensure processors also erase the data (Section 8(7))【dpdp_act_2023:s8(7)|Section 8(7)]}.
- Provide a notice to the Data Principal before requesting consent, specifying the data, purpose, how rights can be exercised and how to lodge a complaint (Section 5(1))【dpdp_act_2023:s5(1)|Section 5(1)]}.
- For consent given before the Act’s commencement, give a notice as soon as practicable describing the data and purpose, and continue processing only until consent is withdrawn (Section 5(2))【dpdp_act_2023:s5(2)|Section 5(2)]}.

All the above Act provisions are not yet in force as of 9 Oct 2026; they will become effective on 13 May 2027.

In summary, to open a company you must comply with the Companies Act and other general laws (not covered here).  If you intend to register the company as a Consent Manager, the conditions and obligations listed above will apply once the Rules commence on 13 Nov 2026.  If the company will process personal data as a Data Fiduciary, the Act’s obligations will apply from 13 May 2027.

items.question: An online learning platform collects children's names, photos, academic records, and behavioural data. What obligations does the platform have under the DPDP Act?
items.author: claude-code (checked against source text; human review pending)

answer.text: At the date 2026-10-09 none of the provisions that impose specific duties on a Data Fiduciary when processing a child’s personal data are yet in force. Section 9(1) of the Act requires a Data Fiduciary to obtain verifiable parental consent before processing a child’s data, but this provision comes into force on 13 May 2027 [Section 9(1), dpdp_act_2023:s9(1)]. Section 9(3) bans tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising of children, also effective from 13 May 2027 [Section 9(3), dpdp_act_2023:s9(3)]. The Rules provide an illustration of how a Data Fiduciary should verify a parent’s identity before processing a child’s data (Rule 10, Illustration), but the Rules only become applicable on 13 May 2027 [Rule 10, Illustration, dpdp_rules_2025:r10:ill]. The Fourth Schedule lists exemptions for educational institutions and transport providers, but those exemptions and the related provisions are likewise not in force until 13 May 2027 [Fourth Schedule, Part A, row 3, dpdp_rules_2025:sch4:A:3; Fourth Schedule, Part A, row 5, dpdp_rules_2025:sch4:A:5]. Section 1(2) confirms that different provisions may commence on different dates [Section 1(2), dpdp_act_2023:s1(2)]. Consequently, as of 9 Oct 2026 the online learning platform is not yet legally required to obtain verifiable parental consent or to refrain from behavioural monitoring of children under the DPDP Act, but those obligations will become binding on 13 May 2027 when the relevant provisions enter into force.

items.question: Can a user withdraw consent, and how easy must it be?
items.author: claude-code (checked against source text; human review pending)

answer.text: Yes. Under Section 6(4) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 a Data Principal may withdraw consent at any time, and the withdrawal must be as easy as the manner in which the consent was originally given. However, this provision is not yet in force on the as‑of date (it will become effective on 13 May 2027). Section 6(5) further explains that withdrawal does not affect the legality of prior processing, but it likewise is not yet in force until 13 May 2027.
